newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: BOE's Davies says 1999 EMU still not certain.
newsitem.headline: BOE's Davies says 1999 EMU still not certain.

text.p: The deputy governor of the Bank of England, Howard Davies, said Monday it is still not certain that Europe's single currency will be introduced as planned in January 1999.

"The plans in place to meet the criteria depend on both political commitments and economic recovery, which governments cannot simply decree," said Davies in a prepared text released to journalists before a speech to a banking forum. He stressed that convergence, such as improving deficits, "should be sustainable over the medium term. So medium-term fiscal improvement is necessary, rather than one-off budget cuts."
He argued that fulfillment of the criteria needs to take place on a sustained basis, "not simply in one benchmark year."
He added that "in fact, there are good grounds for believing that the convergence criteria are not a sufficient condition for safe membership of EMU."
For example, he argued for more labor market flexibility in Europe.
Davies said the only countries that can now be ruled out from joining a single European currency in 1999 are Greece and Denmark.

Up to six months ago, there was a "growing consensus" about the timing and the first members of the single currency. Now, however, some of the countries which were not expected to meet the criteria have made efforts to do so and are closer to joining from the beginning.

"The Portuguese, Spaniards and Italians -- particularly the first two -- have announced plans which, if fully implemented, would give them a much better prospect of qualification when the moment of reckoning arrives in the spring of 1998," Davies said.
In addition, doubts have now emerged about countries previously seen as sure entrants.

"The French and German economies have continued to recover only slowly, unemployment has continued to rise, and the public sector deficits have remained stubbornly high, so determined fiscal measures need to be taken in each case, whose consequences and effectiveness remain uncertain," Davies said.
He said the French general election will generate more uncertainty for a while.
